children.text: The ruins of a Baroque church in San Pablo, Isabela, traditionally said to date to 1624, have been declared a National Cultural Treasure by the National Museum. The façade and a six-tier bell tower still stand, and recent photos show the old nave roofed over with pews. It makes an easy stop on a trip through the northern Cagayan Valley.

The San Pablo Church Ruins are the remains of a Catholic church in the town of San Pablo, Isabela, in the Cagayan Valley of northeastern Luzon. English Wikipedia and the Isabela provincial tourism pages say the church was built in 1624 and is the oldest church in Isabela. Sources do not fully agree on the date, however. Another source says Dominican friar Pedro de Santo Tomas founded it in 1625, and a further account says the structure you see today was built in 1709 by Fr. Diego de la Torre. On site, it is enough to remember that the church dates to the 1620s and that the finer details vary from source to source.

The town was once called Cabagan and is said to have served for a time as the center of Cagayan province. During the Spanish colonial era the Dominicans founded mission towns across the Cagayan Valley, and a church and convent rose here. A fire is also recorded to have destroyed the Cabagan church and convent in 1709, so the building was probably rebuilt more than once. In the twentieth century the town was renamed San Pablo after its patron saint, and the church still carries the dedication to St. Paul the Apostle.

The church took on its present ruined look in the mid-twentieth century. Japanese bombing during World War II badly damaged the building, a magnitude 7 earthquake that shook the Cagayan Valley on December 27, 1949 brought down what was left, and a fire burned off the roof a few years later. Because restoration was not feasible, a small church about one-third the size of the original was built inside the old walls in the 1950s. For a time the façade, the bell tower, the roofless nave turned grassy garden and a small church all shared one site. Photos from 2025–2026, however, show a steel-truss roof over the nave with pews and Mass being held, so the roof appears to have been restored in between (the date is not confirmed).

The style is classed as Baroque, and the walls are described as a mix of brick, river stones, adobe (tuff blocks) and coral stone. Unlike most other colonial churches in the Cagayan Valley, which rely mainly on red brick, this one is notable for its heavy use of adobe. The six-tier bell tower is crowned with a round adobe cap and was once the tallest in the Cagayan Valley. For these qualities the National Museum of the Philippines declared the church a National Cultural Treasure. However, one account notes that no full-scale restoration program had begun even after the designation, so please check the current condition from up-to-date sources before you go. San Pablo is not a developed tourist attraction but a village church beside the highway. No ticket booth or visitor center has been confirmed, and local residents use it for worship as usual. Its charm lies less in facilities than in the quiet time you can spend among old stone walls and beneath the tower. It suits best as a one- to two-hour stop on the way down from Tuguegarao into Isabela or up from Manila.

The two-tier façade has a semicircular arched entrance, and the niches on either side are known to have held statues of St. Paul, St. Vincent Ferrer and St. Isidore. The carvings are now badly defaced. The upper tier still shows clay insets of rosettes and sun emblems, an undulating pediment and a round window.

The square bell tower to the right of the church rises in six tiers of adobe blocks and is topped with a rounded cap. The Isabela provincial government describes it as the tallest in the Cagayan Valley. It can be seen from the highway, so it works as a landmark on the way in. Some stones have chipped away, so please admire it from the ground and do not climb it.

blocks.title: The old nave (before and after the roof)

children.text: Step through the arched entrance into the old nave. Material from 2013–2020 shows it roofless and grassy, but recent photos show a steel-truss roof and pews, so check the current state on site. You can make out the arch that supported the choir loft, the vigil room and traces of the buttresses.

blocks.title: The small active church within the old walls

children.text: The small church built in the 1950s at about one-third of the original size is still where the villagers worship. Visitors report that the interior can be dim and that the sacristan may switch on the lights for you. Please stay quiet during Mass and ask permission before taking photos.

The National Museum of the Philippines has declared the church a National Cultural Treasure. By law this makes it a priority for restoration and government funding, but according to Wikipedia no full restoration has started. The weight of time on the damaged building is itself part of the reason to visit.

blocks.title: Feast of St. Paul and the Baka Festival

children.text: Around the feast of St. Paul the Apostle on
January 15

, San Pablo is said to hold the Baka (cow) Festival, which began in 2004. The schedule and program can change each year, so please check the latest announcements from the Isabela provincial tourism office or the town hall.

The town is presented as the oldest in Isabela, and it is said to have been a center of Cagayan province in earlier times. Standing in front of the church and picturing the Spanish missionaries arriving along the Cagayan River to found towns is a meaningful visit in itself.

items.title: 1–2 hour stopover course
items.subtitle: A stop along the national highway between Tuguegarao and Isabela

children.text: Travel from Tuguegarao or Ilagan along the national highway to San Pablo. The church is said to sit about
from the highway inside the village, so check your drop-off point in advance.
Walk in toward the bell tower you can see from the highway, and examine the arched entrance and clay decoration at the foot of the façade.
Go through the arched door and walk the old nave. Look for the arch that held up the choir loft, the vigil room and traces of the buttresses.
Visit the active church to pray quietly or look around inside. If Mass is in progress, wait outside.
Have lunch in town, then head toward Tuguegarao or Ilagan.
If you are linking this with other stops, about an hour is enough for this one.

items.title: Half-day Cagayan Valley church tour
items.subtitle: Visiting Isabela's colonial churches in sequence

children.text: Set out from Ilagan or Tuguegarao to tour Isabela's old churches one after another.
See another colonial church in the same region first, such as the Tumauini church.
Arrive at the San Pablo Church Ruins and take your time with the façade, bell tower and garden.
Continue to Tuguegarao and on to Cagayan attractions such as Callao Cave.
Opening hours differ from church to church, and visits may be restricted during Mass, so check before you travel.
You can fly from Manila to Tuguegarao Airport (TUG) and continue overland south toward San Pablo. Airlines and flight times change often, so check on a booking site.
From the airport, one guide suggests taking a tricycle to a bus or van terminal heading toward Cabagan or Santiago City and asking to be let off at San Pablo.
Take a Tuguegarao-bound bus from Manila and tell the driver or conductor to drop you off at San Pablo. One blog names Victory Liner, Florida and Dalin as examples and gives the trip as about
10–12 hours
. That post dates from 2010, so check current routes and timetables.
The road distance from Manila to San Pablo is given as about
, depending on the source.
A night bus arrives in the early morning, so plan your lodging and onward transport in advance.
From Ilagan, the provincial capital of Isabela, San Pablo is about
away, depending on the source. You can use a rental car or a local van.
The ruins stand about
from the highway, so you can get off and walk in. Visitors mention that the tower is visible from the road and that there is a sign for the church.

Isabela is reported to have daytime highs of about 28–35 degrees Celsius, nighttime lows of about 19–24 degrees and annual rainfall of about 1,650 mm. February is the driest month, and August to October the wettest.

This is an outdoor site with little shade. We recommend visiting in the morning or when the sun is lower, avoiding midday heat and heavy rains in the wet season. Village events may take place around the feast of St. Paul on January 15.

San Pablo itself has few tourist accommodations, so it is easiest to stay in a city such as Ilagan or Tuguegarao and visit as a day trip. Both cities offer a good choice of hotels and restaurants.

Village eateries serve home-style dishes, grilled food and soups common in Isabela and the Cagayan Valley. Restaurant names change often, so pick whichever place looks good when you arrive. A simple lunch in the village or at a roadside stop after your church visit is a sensible plan.
The church is close to the national highway, so you can get off at the roadside and walk in. When you board a bus, tell the crew in advance to drop you at San Pablo.
Because it is an active church, keep quiet during Mass and dress modestly rather than in shorts or sleeveless tops.
Visitors say the interior can be dark, so try asking the sacristan to turn on the lights.
If your time is short, about an hour is enough, and you can combine the visit with the Tumauini church or Callao Cave.
There is little shade at midday, so bring a hat, water and sunscreen.

Before you go, you can contact the Isabela Provincial Tourism Office (Provincial Capitol Complex, Ilagan) to check on access. The provincial tourism office telephone is listed as (078) 323-3146, but please confirm the latest number.
For photos, the front lawn, where you can frame the façade and bell tower together, works best in morning light.
The distance from Manila is long, so it is most efficient to plan this stop as part of a trip through the northern Cagayan Valley.
The bell tower and walls are old and their stone has chipped, so do not climb or lean on them. Because it is an active church, take care not to disturb worship.
Visitors have long reported that the tower's stones are chipped and dangerous, so do not climb it.
No confirmed information on admission fees or opening hours is available, so check locally before you go.
Bus routes and fares change often, and the 2010 account may be out of date.
In the rainy season, typhoons and heavy rain can block roads, so check the latest weather and road conditions.
Do not touch or write on the façade carvings and walls. This is a National Cultural Treasure.
The central city of Cagayan province, with an airport, it is the starting point for northern Isabela trips. It lies to the north of San Pablo.
The signature cave of Peñablanca, Cagayan, it pairs well with a stop here from Tuguegarao. You can combine it with the church tour in a single day.
Another colonial-era church in Isabela, well worth seeing along the same route. Some itineraries have you stop there before San Pablo.
